prompt: What does a steady red traffic light mean?
choices: Stop completely before the stop line, crosswalk, or intersection
Slow down and continue if no cross traffic is coming
Stop only if other vehicles are already in the intersection
Yield to cross traffic without needing to come to a stop
explanation: A steady red light means stop. Stop before the marked stop line; if there is none, stop before the crosswalk, and if there is no crosswalk, before entering the intersection.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 11, TX p. 31, CA p. 39)

prompt: What does a steady yellow traffic light tell you?
choices: Speed up to get through before the light turns red
The light is about to turn red, so stop if you can do so safely
The signal is malfunctioning, so treat it as a stop sign
Proceed with caution because cross traffic must yield to you
explanation: A steady yellow light warns that the signal is about to turn red. Stop if you can do so safely; speeding up to beat the light is dangerous.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 31, CA p. 39, FL p. 59)

prompt: The light turns yellow when you are so close to the intersection that you cannot stop safely. What should you do?
choices: Continue through the intersection carefully
Brake hard and stop wherever your vehicle comes to rest
Speed up so you clear the intersection before the red
Stop in the crosswalk and wait for the next green
explanation: If you cannot stop safely before the intersection when the light turns yellow, proceed through it with caution. Slamming on the brakes can cause a rear-end crash, and speeding up adds risk.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 31, PA p. 11, CA p. 39)

prompt: You are already inside the intersection when the signal turns yellow. What should you do?
choices: Stop right where you are and wait for green
Back up behind the stop line
Turn on your hazard lights and wait for cross traffic to pass
Continue and clear the intersection with care
explanation: Once you are in the intersection, keep going and clear it carefully. Stopping or backing up inside the intersection blocks traffic and invites a crash.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 11, CA p. 39, AZ p. 35)

prompt: What does a steady green traffic light mean?
choices: You have the right-of-way over everyone, including pedestrians
You must stop first, then go when it is safe
Go if the way is clear, yielding to anyone still crossing
You may only go straight; turns require a green arrow
explanation: A steady green means go, but only when the way is clear. You must still yield to pedestrians and vehicles that are lawfully in the intersection. Turns are allowed on green unless a sign or signal prohibits them.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 31, FL p. 59, PA p. 11)

prompt: You want to turn left at an intersection with a steady green light and no arrow. What must you do?
choices: Turn immediately because a green light protects your turn
Wait until the light turns yellow, then turn no matter what
Stop and wait for a green arrow before turning
Yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, then turn
explanation: A steady green allows a left turn, but it is not protected. You must yield to oncoming vehicles and pedestrians before turning.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 31, FL p. 59, PA p. 11)

prompt: Your light turns green, but traffic is backed up on the far side of the intersection and there is no room for your car. What should you do?
choices: Enter the intersection anyway because you have a green light
Pull into the intersection so you are ready when traffic moves
Go around the backed-up traffic using the shoulder
Wait until there is room to get all the way across
explanation: Do not enter an intersection unless you can get completely across before the light changes. A car stuck in the middle blocks cross traffic and pedestrians when the light turns red.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 40, FL p. 59)

prompt: Your light has just turned green and you are first in line. What should you do before pulling forward?
choices: Go at once, since anyone still crossing must yield to you
Sound your horn to warn cross traffic, then go
Make sure no one is still crossing the intersection
Wait for the driver behind you to signal that it is clear
explanation: A green light lets you go only when the way is clear. Look for vehicles finishing their movement, drivers racing to beat the red, and pedestrians still in the crosswalk.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 31, FL p. 59)

prompt: What does a steady green arrow mean?
choices: You must yield to oncoming traffic before turning
The turn is about to end, so prepare to stop
You may go in any direction from that lane
You may make a protected move in the arrow's direction
explanation: A green arrow gives a protected movement in the direction it points, because conflicting traffic faces a red light. You still yield to any vehicles or pedestrians already in the intersection.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 40, PA p. 11, FL p. 60)

prompt: You are in the left-turn lane. The signal shows a steady red light together with a green arrow pointing left. What may you do?
choices: Turn left, yielding to anyone still in the intersection
Go straight or turn left, because one green light is showing
Nothing; the red light overrides the arrow
Turn left only after the red light changes to green
explanation: A green arrow shown with a red light lets you move only in the direction of the arrow. Oncoming traffic is stopped, but you still yield to anyone already in the intersection.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 31, NY p. 31, FL p. 60)

prompt: What does a steady yellow arrow mean?
choices: The protected turn is ending; stop if you can do so safely
You may turn after yielding to oncoming traffic
Turns in that direction are prohibited at all times
The green arrow is about to come back on
explanation: A steady yellow arrow warns that the protected green-arrow movement is about to end. Stop if you safely can; if you are already turning or cannot stop safely, complete the turn with caution.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 39, PA p. 11, NY p. 31)

prompt: You approach an intersection and the signal for your lane shows a steady red arrow. What must you do first?
choices: Turn in the direction of the arrow after yielding
Stop before the stop line or crosswalk
Slow down and turn if no one is coming
Merge into a lane with a green light and go straight
explanation: A steady red arrow means stop and do not make the movement shown by the arrow while it is red. A few states allow certain turns on a red arrow after a full stop, so learn your state's rule, but you must always stop first.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 39, NY p. 31, FL p. 60, IL p. 81)

prompt: What does a flashing yellow arrow for left turns mean?
choices: Yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, then turn left
Your left turn is protected, so oncoming traffic is stopped
You must stop and wait for a green arrow before turning
Left turns are not allowed until the arrow stops flashing
explanation: A flashing yellow arrow allows a permitted (unprotected) left turn. Oncoming traffic may be moving, so yield to it and to pedestrians before turning.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 31, PA p. 12, CO p. 10, AZ p. 35)

prompt: Why is a left turn on a flashing yellow arrow riskier than one on a green arrow?
choices: Oncoming traffic may have a green light at the same time
Pedestrians are not allowed to cross during a flashing yellow arrow
The flashing yellow arrow means the signal is broken
Drivers behind you are allowed to pass you on the left
explanation: During a flashing yellow arrow, your turn is not protected because oncoming traffic usually has a green light. With a green arrow, oncoming traffic is stopped.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 12, FL p. 60, CA p. 40)

prompt: What does a flashing red traffic light mean?
choices: Slow down and proceed with caution without stopping
Stop and wait until the light turns green
The signal is about to turn green
Stop completely, then go when it is safe
explanation: A flashing red light has the same meaning as a STOP sign: come to a full stop, yield as required, then proceed when it is safe.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 12, TX p. 31, CA p. 39, NY p. 31)

prompt: What does a flashing yellow traffic light mean?
choices: Come to a full stop, then proceed
The light is about to turn red
You have the right-of-way and may keep your speed
Slow down and proceed with caution
explanation: A flashing yellow light is a warning: slow down, be alert, and proceed carefully. You do not need to stop unless traffic or pedestrians require it.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 40, PA p. 12, TX p. 31)

prompt: You face a flashing red light. Drivers on the cross street have a flashing yellow light. What should you expect?
choices: Traffic in every direction must stop, as at an all-way stop
You may go first because red outranks yellow
You must stop and yield; cross traffic may not stop for you
Cross traffic must stop and wave you through
explanation: A flashing red means stop, then go when safe. Drivers facing a flashing yellow only slow down and proceed with caution, so the intersecting traffic may not have to stop.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 31, PA p. 12)

prompt: You come to an intersection where the traffic signals are completely dark because of a power failure. What should you do?
choices: Slow down and drive through like a green light
Treat it like an all-way stop
Yield only to vehicles on your right without stopping
Stop only if a police officer is present
explanation: When a traffic signal is not working, stop as if there were STOP signs in all directions, then proceed when it is safe, following right-of-way rules.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 40, PA p. 12, NJ p. 70, NY p. 30)

prompt: You are on a busy main road and the signal ahead is dark during a power outage. What is correct?
choices: Main-road drivers keep going; only side-street drivers stop
Every driver must stop, including those on the main road
Drivers on the main road should slow down and sound their horn
Whoever is going faster has the right-of-way
explanation: A non-working signal is treated as an all-way stop for every approach, not just the side streets. After stopping, follow the normal right-of-way rules.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 35, CO p. 10, NY p. 30, NJ p. 70)

prompt: A traffic signal shows green for you, but a police officer at the intersection signals you to stop. What should you do?
choices: Go, because the green light takes priority
Slow down and continue if the intersection looks clear
Stop and follow the officer's directions
Honk to get the officer's attention, then go
explanation: Directions from a police officer or authorized traffic controller override traffic signals, signs, and pavement markings.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 33, TX p. 31)

prompt: On a standard vertical traffic signal, where is the red light?
choices: In the middle
At the top
At the bottom
Its position changes from one intersection to the next
explanation: Traffic lights are arranged in a standard order. On a vertical signal, red is on top and green is on the bottom; on a horizontal signal, red is on the left. This helps drivers who have trouble telling colors apart.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 11, CO p. 10, NY p. 30)

prompt: What does a pedestrian signal showing a walking person or the word WALK mean?
choices: Pedestrians must hurry because the light is about to change
Pedestrians may start crossing in the direction of the signal
Pedestrians must wait for turning cars to finish
Drivers turning across the crosswalk have the right-of-way
explanation: The WALK or walking-person signal means pedestrians may begin crossing. Drivers turning across that crosswalk must yield to them.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 41, PA p. 13, FL p. 63)

prompt: What does a steady DON'T WALK signal or steady raised hand mean for pedestrians?
choices: Cross quickly before traffic starts
Cross only if no cars are turning
Do not start crossing the street
Wait in the middle of the street
explanation: A steady DON'T WALK or raised hand means pedestrians may not enter the street in that direction.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 41, FL p. 63, AK p. 57)

prompt: A pedestrian is halfway across the street when the raised hand starts flashing. What should the pedestrian do?
choices: Turn around and return to the starting curb
Stop and wait in the lane until the WALK signal returns
Continue and finish crossing
Wave drivers on and cross between their cars
explanation: A flashing DON'T WALK or raised hand warns that the crossing time is ending. Pedestrians already in the street should finish crossing.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 13, FL p. 63, NV p. 31)

prompt: What do the numbers on a pedestrian countdown signal show?
choices: How many seconds until drivers get a green light
How many pedestrians may cross at one time
How many seconds are left to finish crossing
How many seconds until the WALK signal returns
explanation: A countdown signal displays the seconds remaining in the crossing time. When it reaches zero, the steady DON'T WALK or raised hand appears.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 41, FL p. 63, AK p. 57)

prompt: Your light turns green as the pedestrian signal changes to a flashing raised hand. A pedestrian is still in the crosswalk in front of you. What should you do?
choices: Go, because the flashing hand means the pedestrian must yield
Honk so the pedestrian hurries out of your way
Drive around the pedestrian if there is room
Wait until the pedestrian has crossed safely
explanation: Drivers must yield to pedestrians who are still in the crosswalk, even when the DON'T WALK signal is flashing and your light is green.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 41, FL p. 59)

prompt: You are turning right on a green light. Pedestrians are crossing the street you are turning onto with a WALK signal. What should you do?
choices: Turn quickly in front of them while there is a gap
Turn, since your green light gives you the right-of-way
Wait for the pedestrians to cross before completing your turn
Sound your horn and turn slowly through the crosswalk
explanation: Pedestrians crossing with a WALK signal have the right-of-way over turning vehicles. A green light does not let you drive through an occupied crosswalk.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 11, FL p. 59, TX p. 31)

prompt: You approach a marked crosswalk in the middle of a block. An overhead beacon above it shows a steady red light. What should you do?
choices: Slow down and go if you do not see anyone
Stop and stay stopped while pedestrians cross
Proceed, because the beacon is only for pedestrians
Stop briefly, then go even if people are still crossing
explanation: Pedestrian hybrid beacons stop traffic at crosswalks when a pedestrian pushes the button. A steady red indication means stop for pedestrians in the crosswalk.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 30, FL p. 63, NE p. 41, GA p. 36)

prompt: An overhead pedestrian beacon above a midblock crosswalk is completely dark. What does this usually mean?
choices: No one has pushed the button; drive on with normal care
The signal has failed, so treat it as an all-way stop
You must stop and wait for it to turn on
The crosswalk is closed and pedestrians may not use it
explanation: A pedestrian hybrid beacon stays dark until a pedestrian presses the button. Dark means continue with normal caution; it is not a broken signal at an intersection.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 30, FL p. 63, GA p. 36)

prompt: A steady red X is lit over a lane. What does it mean?
choices: The lane is open to all traffic
Do not drive in that lane
The lane is about to open, so move into it
Drive in the lane only to pass
explanation: A red X lane-use signal means you may not drive in the lane under it. Opposing traffic may be using it.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 38, PA p. 12, FL p. 61, NY p. 31)

prompt: A green arrow pointing down is lit over a lane. What does it mean?
choices: The lane is closed ahead
You may drive in that lane
You must exit the highway from that lane
The lane is reserved for turning vehicles only
explanation: A steady downward green arrow over a lane means the lane is open to you. You must still obey all other signs and signals.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 38, PA p. 12, FL p. 61)

prompt: A steady yellow X appears over the lane you are driving in. What should you do?
choices: Use caution and get ready to move out of the lane safely
Stop in the lane until a green arrow appears
Speed up to finish using the lane before it closes
Keep driving in the lane; yellow X signals apply only to trucks
explanation: A steady yellow X warns that the lane's use is changing, usually to a red X. Slow down, use caution, and prepare to move safely to an open lane.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 38, PA p. 12, FL p. 61, NY p. 31)

prompt: You are driving in a reversible lane and see a red X lit over your lane ahead. What should you do?
choices: Stay in the lane, since the red X is meant for oncoming traffic
Stop where you are and wait for the X to turn green
Turn on your hazard lights and continue to the next exit
Move safely into a lane with a green arrow
explanation: A red X means you must not drive in that lane, often because oncoming traffic will be using it. Move safely to an open lane.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 38, AK p. 58, NV p. 37)

prompt: The red lights are flashing at a railroad crossing. What must you do?
choices: Slow down and cross quickly before the train arrives
Cross if you look both ways and do not see a train
Stop only if the gates are down
Stop, because a train is coming
explanation: Flashing red lights at a railroad crossing mean a train is coming. Stop and stay stopped until it is safe to cross.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 13, FL p. 64, NJ p. 78)

prompt: A train has passed, but the crossing gates are still down and the lights are still flashing. What should you do?
choices: Wait until the gates rise and the lights stop
Drive around the gates, since the train is gone
Cross carefully if the tracks look clear both ways
Back up and look for another way across the tracks
explanation: Never drive around or under crossing gates. Wait until the gates are fully raised and the lights have stopped flashing before crossing.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 39, NJ p. 78, FL p. 64, AK p. 63)

prompt: At a crossing with two sets of tracks, a train passes but the lights keep flashing. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The signal is stuck and can be ignored
The lights flash for a set time after every train
A second train may be coming on another track
The gate is broken and drivers may go around it
explanation: Watch out for a second train. When the last car passes, do not start until you are sure no train is coming on another track, often from the other direction.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AK p. 63, AL p. 42, CO p. 24)

prompt: What does a large X with the letters R and R painted on the road mean?
choices: A reversible lane begins ahead
A railroad crossing is ahead
Right turns are restricted at the next intersection
A rest area is coming up
explanation: The "R X R" pavement marking is placed on the approach to a railroad crossing to warn drivers to look, listen, and be ready to stop.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 26, GA p. 37, CO p. 24)

prompt: What do yellow lines on the road separate?
choices: Lanes of traffic moving in the same direction
Parking spaces from the travel lane
Bicycle lanes from car lanes
Traffic moving in opposite directions
explanation: Yellow lines separate traffic traveling in opposite directions. White lines separate lanes going the same direction and mark the right edge of the road.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 26, NY p. 32, FL p. 52)

prompt: What do white lane lines between lanes separate?
choices: Lanes of traffic moving in the same direction
Traffic moving in opposite directions on a highway
No-passing zones on two-lane roads
Lanes that are closed to traffic
explanation: White lines divide lanes of traffic moving the same way. Yellow lines are used where traffic moves in opposite directions.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 32, CA p. 19, CO p. 12)

prompt: What does a broken (dashed) lane line mean?
choices: You may cross it when it is safe
You may never cross it, even to pass
You may cross it only to make a U-turn
It marks the edge of the road and the shoulder
explanation: Broken lines may be crossed to pass or change lanes, but only when it is safe and does not interfere with other traffic.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 40, NY p. 32, PA p. 26)

prompt: What does a double solid yellow center line mean?
choices: Passing is not allowed in either direction
Passing is allowed for traffic on the left side only
Passing is allowed if no oncoming traffic is visible
The road is a one-way street
explanation: Double solid yellow lines mark the center of a two-way road where neither direction may cross them to pass.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 26, CA p. 19, FL p. 52)

prompt: On a two-lane road, the center line has a solid yellow line next to the oncoming lane and a broken yellow line next to your lane. Are you allowed to pass?
choices: No, because any solid line means no passing for both directions
Only if the oncoming driver flashes their headlights at you
No, because yellow lines can never be crossed
Yes, when it is safe, because the broken line is on your side
explanation: With a solid-and-broken yellow center line, the line closest to you controls. If the broken line is on your side, you may pass when it is safe.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 26, FL p. 52, NY p. 32)

prompt: The center line on your two-lane road is a solid yellow line on your side and a broken yellow line on the other side. What does this mean for you?
choices: You may pass if the road ahead looks clear
You may pass only on hills and curves
Oncoming drivers may not pass
You may not pass
explanation: A solid yellow line on your side of the center line marks a no-passing zone for you. Drivers on the broken-line side may pass when safe.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 40, PA p. 26, FL p. 52)

prompt: You enter a divided highway and notice a solid yellow line on your RIGHT and a solid white line on your LEFT. What does this most likely mean?
choices: You are driving the wrong way
You are in the correct lane next to the median
You are in a reversible lane
You are in a lane reserved for passing
explanation: On a divided highway, the left edge of your side is marked with yellow and the right edge with white. If the yellow line is on your right, you are facing the wrong direction and must get off the road safely.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 26, TX p. 40)

prompt: What does a solid white line along the right side of the road mark?
choices: A lane you may use for passing on the right
The center line of a two-way road
The start of a bicycle-only lane
The edge of the road, where the shoulder begins
explanation: A solid white edge line shows where the travel lane ends and the shoulder begins. Do not drive across it except where allowed.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 31, PA p. 26, CO p. 12)

prompt: An edge line ahead angles in toward the center of the road. What does this tell you?
choices: The road narrows ahead
A passing lane is starting
The shoulder is open for travel
A turn lane is about to open on the right
explanation: An edge line that angles toward the center of the road shows that the roadway becomes narrower ahead.
ref: New York Driver's Manual, p. 31

prompt: What does a double solid white line between two lanes mean?
choices: You may cross it to pass slower traffic
Do not cross it to change lanes
It separates traffic moving in opposite directions
You may cross it only at night
explanation: Double solid white lines mean lane changes across them are not allowed. They are often used next to carpool lanes and near ramps; wait for a broken line to change lanes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 40, CA p. 20, FL p. 51)

prompt: What does a single solid white line between two lanes going the same direction mean?
choices: Lane changes across it are encouraged when traffic is heavy
It separates traffic moving in opposite directions
Stay in your lane; avoid changing lanes across it
It shows that the lane on the other side is closed
explanation: A single solid white line between same-direction lanes means stay in your lane. Some states allow crossing it in limited cases, such as to avoid a hazard, but it is not a normal place to change lanes; wait for a broken line.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 51, CO p. 12, AK p. 61, AL p. 54)

prompt: Wide, closely spaced broken (dotted) white lines appear along your lane on a freeway. What should you be ready for?
choices: A carpool lane is starting on your left
Your lane may end or become exit-only
A lane that is shared with oncoming traffic
A lane where you may stop or park
explanation: Wider, more closely spaced broken lines are often used to mark lanes that end or exit. Look for signs telling you to exit or merge.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 20, NV p. 32)

prompt: A wide white line is painted across your lane at a red light. Where should you stop?
choices: Behind the line
With your front wheels on the line
Just past the line, before the crosswalk
Anywhere you can see cross traffic
explanation: A white stop line shows where you must stop for a stop sign or signal. Stop before any part of your vehicle crosses it.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 40, FL p. 53, NY p. 32)

prompt: You must stop at a red light. There is a marked crosswalk but no stop line. Where should you stop?
choices: In the crosswalk, as long as no one is crossing
Before you reach the crosswalk
At the curb line of the cross street
In the middle of the intersection
explanation: If there is no stop line, stop before the crosswalk. If there is no crosswalk either, stop before entering the intersection.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 40, NY p. 32, PA p. 11)

prompt: What do white lines or stripes painted across a road at an intersection usually mark?
choices: A speed bump
A place where parking is allowed
The end of a no-passing zone
A crosswalk where pedestrians cross
explanation: Crosswalk lines show where pedestrians should cross. Drivers must yield to pedestrians in a crosswalk and stop before it when required.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 40, FL p. 53, NY p. 32)

prompt: A row of white triangles is painted across your lane, with the points facing you. What does it mean?
choices: Speed bumps are ahead
The lane is reserved for buses
Yield here, and stop if needed
Pass on either side
explanation: A yield line ("shark teeth") is a row of white triangles pointing toward approaching vehicles. It shows where to yield or stop.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 20, PA p. 26)

prompt: Your lane has a curved left arrow and the word ONLY painted on it. What must you do?
choices: Turn left from that lane
Go straight or turn left
Turn left only if the light is green
Use the lane to pass, then return to the right
explanation: A lane marked with a turn arrow and the word ONLY is reserved for that turn. Drivers in the lane must turn in the direction of the arrow.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 53, PA p. 26, NY p. 32)

prompt: A lane is marked with both a straight arrow and a curved right arrow. What may you do from that lane?
choices: Only turn right
Only go straight
Turn right only on a red light
Either go straight or turn right
explanation: When a lane shows both a straight arrow and a turn arrow, you may either continue straight or make that turn.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 53, NY p. 32)

prompt: Close to an intersection, you realize your lane is marked for right turns only, but you wanted to go straight. A solid white line separates you from the next lane. What should you do?
choices: Cross the solid line and squeeze into the straight lane
Stop in the lane until someone lets you over
Turn right, then find another route
Go straight from the right-turn lane if no one is beside you
explanation: You must be in the correct lane before reaching the solid line that separates the lanes. If you are in a turn-only lane, make the turn and recover safely afterward.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 32, FL p. 53)

prompt: A center lane is bordered on each side by a solid yellow line on the outside and a broken yellow line on the inside. What is it for?
choices: Passing slower vehicles in either direction
Left turns by traffic from both directions
Emergency and service vehicles only
Through traffic during rush hour
explanation: This is a two-way left-turn lane. Drivers from either direction may use it to slow down and make a left turn.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 48, CA p. 22, PA p. 26)

prompt: You are behind a slow truck on a road that has a two-way center left-turn lane. Is it okay to use the center lane to pass the truck?
choices: Yes, if no one is turning in the center lane
No, the center lane is only for making left turns
Yes, but only for a short distance
Yes, if you signal first
explanation: A two-way left-turn lane is not a travel or passing lane. Use it only to prepare for and make a left turn, and watch for drivers from the other direction using it too.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 48, CA p. 22, TX p. 39)

prompt: What does a white diamond painted in a lane usually mean?
choices: The lane is closed for construction ahead
The lane is for slow-moving vehicles only
A railroad crossing is ahead in this lane
It is a reserved lane, such as a carpool lane
explanation: A diamond symbol marks a reserved lane, such as a high-occupancy vehicle (HOV) or bus lane. Signs tell you who may use it and when.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 22, NY p. 33, AZ p. 33)

prompt: When may you drive in a lane marked with white diamonds?
choices: Any time you need to pass a slower vehicle
Only at night, when traffic is light
When you meet the rules posted on its signs
Never; diamond lanes are for emergency vehicles only
explanation: Diamond-marked lanes are reserved for vehicles that meet the occupancy or other requirements shown on signs, during the hours shown.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 33, CA p. 22, AZ p. 33)

prompt: A lane is separated from traffic by a solid white line and has a bicycle symbol painted in it. What is it?
choices: An extra lane for slow-moving cars
A shoulder you may use to pass on the right
A bike lane, not a travel lane for cars
A lane for parking when no bikes are present
explanation: Bike lanes are marked with a solid white line and often a bicycle symbol or sign. Drivers may not use them as regular travel lanes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 23, FL p. 53)

prompt: You are about to turn right, and a marked bike lane runs between your lane and the curb. What must you do?
choices: Turn quickly so you get ahead of any bicyclists
Honk to warn bicyclists, then turn
Check for bicyclists and yield to any in the bike lane before entering or crossing it
Turn from the lane you are in without looking, since bike lanes end at intersections
explanation: Drivers may enter or cross a bike lane to turn only when no bicyclist is in the way. Check mirrors and your blind spot and yield to bicyclists.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 53, CA p. 24, NE p. 54)

prompt: Part of a lane or intersection is painted bright green. What does this usually mean?
choices: It is a lane for electric cars only
It marks a bicycle area; watch for bicyclists
It is a lane reserved for buses and taxis
It marks the start of a school zone
explanation: Green pavement is used to highlight bike lanes and areas where bicyclists and drivers cross paths, making bicyclists easier to notice.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 12, CA p. 23, NY p. 70)

prompt: A bicycle symbol with two arrowheads (a "sharrow") is painted in a regular travel lane. What does it mean?
choices: Bicycles are not allowed in this lane
Bicyclists and drivers share the lane
This is a bike-only lane that cars must avoid
Bicyclists must ride on the shoulder next to it
explanation: Shared lane markings tell drivers that bicyclists may use the travel lane and show bicyclists where to ride.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 53, CO p. 12, AL p. 52)

prompt: At a freeway exit, a triangle-shaped area between the exit ramp and the main lanes is outlined with white lines and filled with stripes. What should you do?
choices: Do not drive across it, stop in it, or park in it
Use it to change lanes if you are about to miss the exit
Use it as a place to pull over and check directions
Drive across it only if traffic is light
explanation: This striped area is called a gore area. Do not drive over it or park in it; if you miss your exit, continue to the next one.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 32, GA p. 41, FL p. 53)

prompt: In general, what does a painted curb tell drivers?
choices: Parking there is allowed at any time
The lane next to it is for passing only
Special parking or stopping rules apply
Pedestrians may not use the sidewalk there
explanation: Curb colors signal parking or stopping restrictions, such as no parking near a fire hydrant. The exact meaning of each color can differ by state, so check your state's rules.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 53, CA p. 34)
